newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Military officials say Israel hurt by defence cuts.
newsitem.headline: Military officials say Israel hurt by defence cuts.

text.p: Israeli military officials on Thursday condemned the government's decision to cut defence spending, saying it could hurt the Jewish state in any new Middle East war.
But some analysts said if efficiency measures were imposed, the army could afford to slash more.

The cabinet approved an 800 million shekel ($228 million) cut in the 1997 budget on Wednesday to keep to its 2.8 percent deficit target. The defence ministry was pinched for nearly 206 million shekels -- more than any other government office.

"This government declared it would increase security and increasing security...also means increasing resources," said Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, who boycotted Wednesday's cabinet meeting to protest against the cuts.
"I certainly regret the harm done (to the military)," he told reporters on Thursday.
Other officials pointed to assessments this year by military intelligence officers that the risk of war with Syria had increased.

Israeli-Syrian peace talks have been dormant since December 1995 when negotiators failed to solve the core dispute -- the fate of the Golan Heights which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war and Syria wants back.
Netanyahu wants to keep all of the strategic plateau, raising fears Syria might use force to retreive what it has failed to get at the bargaining table.
"The assessments about an increased chance of war require that the budget be increased, not slashed," defence ministry economic adviser Imri Tov told Reuters.
Israel has fought several wars with its Arab neighbours and still keeps thousands of troops in the West Bank, Gaza, Golan and south Lebanon.
Tension with Damascus soared last year when President Hafez al-Assad moved thousands of his troops stationed in Lebanon to within striking distance of the Golan.
The cut flew in the face of promises by Netanyahu to raise the 30 billion shekel defence budget, and dented hopes in the military for a 1.5 billion shekel increase in defence spending next year.

"The real concern in the defence establishment is that this cut points to a trend and that the increase sought for next year will not be approved," military analyst Amnon Barzilai of the Haaretz newspaper said.
He said the cuts could force the army to choose U.S. companies over Israeli firms in defence contracts.

Israel receives $1.8 billion in annual American military aid with a provision that the money be used to buy U.S.-made hardware. Defence spending accounts for about 16 percent of government's 1997 budget.
Other analysts cited operational inefficiency and inflated benefits for career officers as the main reason for the army's budget troubles.
"The claim by the defence minister and army officials that there's nowhere to make cuts in the army is false," said the Haaretz newspaper in its Thursday editorial.
It said around 54 percent of the defence budget went to paying salaries and pensions for troops compared with 33 percent in 1984.
"The army is a big organisation which needs efficiency measures now as much as ever," the newspaper said.
($1 = 3.51 shekels)
